meaning: The number 99 is best known as the age at which Abraham received his covenant with God and was circumcised, symbolizing faithfulness and a divine promise on the threshold of perfection.
description: In Genesis 17 God reveals Himself to Abraham when he is 99 years old, establishes the covenant of circumcision and promises him a son through Sarah. The number stands symbolically on the threshold of 100, which represents completeness and perfection, suggesting that Abraham was nearly at the end of his waiting period before God's promise was fulfilled. In the New Testament the number 99 appears in Jesus' parable of the good shepherd (Matthew 18:12–13), where the 99 sheep are left behind to find the one lost – an image of God's grace and the infinite value of each individual person. The number thus carries a symbolism of divine patience, covenant faithfulness and grace nearing completion.

Jesus' parables are not part of Jewish tradition – they belong to the New Testament and Christian tradition. This formulation is theologically incorrect and should be corrected.; [minor] The parable of the 99 sheep is an important biblical reference point for the number 99, but it should be formulated as a Christian/New Testament tradition, not Jewish tradition.; [minor] The details about the parable of the good shepherd somewhat disrupt the flow of the description, which primarily concerns the Abraham narrative. It may be considered to move this to a footnote, but it is also acceptable to keep it in the main text with proper theological context.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. footnotes.text: In rabbinic tradition, it is emphasized that Abraham was 99 years old—one year short of the 'perfect' 100—when God required circumcision as a sign of the covenant. This timing underscores that God's call can come even when a person feels they have waited to the very limit.

In gematria, the number 99 has been linked to the Hebrew expression אמן (amen), which has a numerical value of 91, not 99. However, some kabbalistic interpretations view 99 as 9×11, where 9 represents completion and 11 signifies transcendence, pointing toward a transcendence of the natural order.

The parable of the 99 sheep appears in two versions: Matthew 18:12–13 and Luke 15:4–7. In Luke's version, the context is Jesus' defense of associating with tax collectors and sinners, while Matthew places it within a discourse on humility and care within the community.
